title: Hall, yard and zones overview
text:
1. Harborwick 3PL Ltd. operates from a single site in Port Sellow, Alveria. The site stores and distributes packed consumer goods — food, drugstore products and household items — for about twenty regular clients. Accuracy of stock on the rack is the basis of our service.

2. The site consists of one single-storey warehouse hall of 6,000 m2 with 10 m clear height, plus a small office annex. All warehousing activity takes place inside the hall. The office annex is separate from storage, picking and driving areas.

3. Outside the hall is a fenced yard of about 3,500 m2. The yard contains our 8 dock doors at 1.2 m dock height, the manoeuvring area for trailers and vans, and a marked driver waiting area. Drivers wait in the waiting area and never enter the hall.

4. Dock doors have fixed directions. Doors 1-4 are inbound only and serve receiving. Doors 5-8 are outbound only and serve dispatch. Every carrier is assigned a door and a time slot by the dispatcher. No truck loads or unloads without that assignment.

5. The hall floor is divided into six fixed zones, A to F. Every employee learns these zones on day one. No zone may be used for another zone's purpose without instruction from the shift supervisor.

6. Zone A — receiving, 800 m2. This zone covers inbound docks 1-4, unloading space and goods inspection. All inbound goods stop in Zone A until documents, quantities and condition are checked. Nothing moves to storage before release.

7. Zone B — bulk storage, 2,200 m2. This is our high-bay pallet racking area with 2,400 pallet positions, plus controlled block-stacking areas. It holds the main reserve stock for all ambient goods. Zone C — picking, 1,200 m2. This zone holds ground-level pick faces and flow racks fed from Zone B. Order picking takes place only here.

8. Zone D — dispatch, 900 m2. This is the outbound staging area in front of docks 5-8. Only wrapped and labelled pallets staged for an assigned door are held here. Zone E — cold zone, 300 m2. This is a separate chilled store held between +2 °C and +6 °C for temperature-sensitive goods.

9. Zone F — services and control, 600 m2. This zone holds value-added packing, quarantine for damaged or suspect goods, and returns inspection. Inside Zone F is a separate ventilated hazmat cage of 60 m2. Hazmat is stored only in that cage and nowhere else on site.

10. Together Zones A to F use the full 6,000 m2 of the hall. Zone boundaries, transport aisles and pedestrian walkways are marked on the floor and must be kept clear. Pallets, equipment or waste must never block a zone boundary, a dock approach or an emergency route.

title: Shifts and supervision
text:
1. Harborwick 3PL Ltd. works two fixed shifts, Monday to Friday. The morning shift runs from 06:00 to 14:00. The afternoon shift runs from 14:00 to 22:00. All regular receiving, storage, picking and dispatch work takes place inside these hours.

2. Outside shift hours the warehouse hall is closed. No picking, put-away, loading or unloading takes place between 22:00 and 06:00, at weekends, or on public holidays, except for approved peak-season overtime. Equipment is parked, dock doors are closed and the site is secured.

3. In peak season the company adds overtime on Saturday mornings. Saturday overtime is limited to a morning session and is used only to clear backlog from the working week or to prepare outbound loads. There is no regular Saturday afternoon, Sunday or night work.

4. Overtime is approved only by the warehouse manager. Shift supervisors, dispatchers and stock controllers cannot authorise overtime. Requests for Saturday working are made in advance, and only staff assigned to the approved overtime session attend the site.

5. Each shift is run by one shift supervisor. There are two shift supervisors in total, one for mornings and one for afternoons. There is always exactly one shift supervisor in charge of the floor during operating hours, including any approved overtime session.

6. The shift supervisor is responsible for all floor staff during the shift. Forklift operators, inbound operators, pickers, stock controllers, returns and packing staff, the maintenance technician, dispatchers and floaters on duty all report to the shift supervisor on shift for task allocation, zone discipline and safety.

7. The shift supervisor is also responsible for immediate incident response on the shift. Any injury, near miss, spill, temperature alarm, equipment fault or damage to racking or goods is reported to the shift supervisor at once, who takes charge of the floor, secures the area and ensures the incident is recorded for follow-up.

8. The warehouse manager is accountable for the whole site across both shifts. The warehouse manager sets staffing levels, approves overtime, holds final sign-off on stocktake results and large write-offs, and authorises new forklift operators. The warehouse manager does not replace the shift supervisor in day-to-day control of the floor.

9. Staffing is planned for about 38 to 40 people in total, with coverage across both shifts. Two floaters cover absence, holidays and peak workload so that each shift remains fully staffed. If absence cannot be covered safely, the shift supervisor adjusts tasks and priorities rather than working short-handed in high-risk areas.

10. Shifts change over at 14:00. The outgoing shift supervisor hands over the floor to the incoming shift supervisor under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Open inbound doors, unfinished put-away or replenishment, staged outbound loads in Zone D, and any incidents or equipment defects are communicated directly so the next shift starts with a clear picture.

title: General floor rules and PPE
text:
1. No person enters or remains on the warehouse floor without mandatory personal protective equipment. High-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear are required for everyone on the floor at all times, with no exceptions for staff, managers or visitors.

2. The high-visibility vest must be worn closed and kept visible. Jackets, bags or other clothing must not cover it while on the floor. Footwear must be laced or fastened correctly. Anyone without correct vest and footwear is refused access to the hall and reports to the shift supervisor.

3. Forklift operators and reach-truck operators wear seat belts whenever the truck is moving. The belt is fastened before driving off and remains fastened until the truck is parked. No truck is driven with a defective or missing belt; the defect is reported at once.

4. Only authorised persons work in operating zones. Floor staff remain in their assigned zone and task area. Drivers, visitors and other non-warehouse staff wait in the marked waiting area and never enter the hall or approach dock doors unless escorted and wearing full PPE.

5. Pedestrians use only the marked pedestrian walkways and crossings. Walkways are 1.2 m wide and physically separated by yellow barriers. Cutting across transport aisles, storage aisles or the dock approaches outside a marked crossing is forbidden.

6. All driving and handling keeps to the marked aisles. Main transport aisles are 4.0 m wide and rack storage aisles are 3.0 m wide. Aisles, walkways, zone boundaries, dock approaches and emergency routes are kept clear at all times and are never blocked by pallets, equipment, packaging or waste.

7. Speed limits apply to every truck and pallet jack on site and are enforced. The limit is 8 km/h inside the building and 12 km/h in the yard, reduced to 5 km/h wherever people and trucks meet, including marked pedestrian zones, crossings and dock ramps. Pedestrians always have priority.

8. Only trained and authorised operators use materials-handling equipment. No employee operates a forklift, reach truck, electric pallet jack, stretch wrapper or baler without instruction for that equipment, and no one operates a forklift or reach truck unless authorised by the warehouse manager. Hand pallet jacks are used only for small moves within their capacity.

9. Housekeeping is part of floor safety. Spills, strapping, foil, cardboard and other trip or slip hazards are cleared immediately and reported to the shift supervisor. Damaged pallets, leaking goods or defective equipment are taken out of use, marked and reported the same shift.

10. Every injury, near miss, spill, alarm, rack impact or equipment fault is reported immediately to the shift supervisor in charge of the floor. The shift supervisor stops unsafe work, secures the area and ensures the event is recorded. Instructions from the shift supervisor on safety, PPE and zone discipline are binding on all persons on the floor.

title: Roles on the floor
text:
1. Harborwick 3PL Ltd. employs around 38 to 40 people on site. The organisation is flat and floor-oriented: one warehouse manager accountable for the site, two shift supervisors running the shifts, and specialist floor teams for inbound, storage, picking, inventory, returns and packing, dispatch, maintenance, and flexible cover.

2. The warehouse manager is accountable for the whole site — operations, safety and final sign-offs. The manager sets shift staffing, work priorities and site rules, holds accountability for stock accuracy and safe operation of the hall, yard and equipment, and provides the final sign-offs defined in ops.ch02.s2. The manager does not take over day-to-day control of the floor from the shift supervisor on shift.

3. There are two shift supervisors, one for the morning shift 06:00-14:00 and one for the afternoon shift 14:00-22:00, including any approved Saturday overtime. The supervisor on shift runs the floor: allocates staff to zones and tasks, enforces zone discipline, PPE and speed rules, and takes charge of immediate incident response. All floor staff on duty report to that supervisor during the shift.

4. Forklift operators, eight in total across both shifts, drive the materials-handling fleet. They operate the counterbalance forklifts, reach trucks and electric pallet jacks for unloading support, put-away to Zone B, replenishment to Zone C, movements to Zone E and Zone F, and staging and loading in Zone D. They work only on equipment they are instructed for and drive forklifts and reach trucks only when authorised by the warehouse manager.

5. Inbound operators, six in total, work in Zone A at inbound docks 1-4. They unload arriving trucks, count and inspect goods, check documents, quantities and condition, and prepare inspected goods for system booking and release to put-away. Nothing leaves Zone A on their watch until the receipt checks are complete.

6. Pickers, ten in total, work in Zone C. They pick customer orders against WMS scanner tasks from ground-level pick faces and flow racks, scan-verify every picked item, and pass picked goods to packing and to Zone D. Before each picking shift they are supplied by replenishment from bulk storage and do not pick from unreplenished or unbooked stock.

7. Stock controllers, two in total, own inventory accuracy day to day. They run the daily cycle counts on the rotating zone schedule, carry out second counts and recounts, investigate discrepancies between system and rack, and prepare adjustments for approval. They work closely with inbound, picking and returns staff to keep the system stock identical to the physical stock.

8. Returns and packing staff, four in total, work in Zone F and at the packing stations. They inspect all returns in Zone F, propose restock, rework or scrap for decision, carry out value-added packing, and support packing and labelling of outbound goods. Damaged or suspect goods found by any team are handed to them for quarantine handling.

9. Dispatchers, two in total, book transport, assign every carrier a dock door and time slot, and release outbound loads. They own the dock schedule for doors 1-4 inbound and doors 5-8 outbound, coordinate drivers in the marked waiting area, and authorise loading and sealing of released loads in Zone D. The maintenance technician maintains trucks, racking and dock equipment and logs every repair.

10. Floaters, two in total, cover absence, holidays and peak workload across zones and shifts. They are trained for basic inbound, picking, packing and dispatch support tasks and are assigned by the shift supervisor where cover is needed. If cover cannot maintain safe staffing in high-risk areas such as dock approaches or high bays, the shift supervisor reprioritises work rather than operating short-handed.

title: Approvals and ownership
text:
1. The warehouse manager is accountable for the whole site — operations, safety and stock accuracy. That accountability cannot be delegated. The manager sets priorities, owns the site rules and procedures PR-01 to PR-15, and provides the final sign-offs listed in this section.

2. The warehouse manager alone signs off the annual wall-to-wall stocktake results. Stock controllers prepare the count, investigate differences and propose adjustments, but no stocktake result becomes final until the manager has reviewed and signed it. The same applies to any cycle-count adjustment that changes system stock.

3. Damaged-goods write-offs are split by value. The shift supervisor approves write-offs up to and including 750 EUR. Any write-off above 750 EUR is reserved to the warehouse manager. No goods are scrapped, removed from stock or written off in value without one of these two written approvals, and the threshold is applied per case, not split to stay below it.

4. Only the warehouse manager approves overtime. This covers any Saturday morning peak-season session and any extension beyond the Monday to Friday shifts 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00. Shift supervisors, dispatchers and stock controllers request overtime but cannot authorise it, and only staff rostered for the approved session may attend.

5. Only the warehouse manager authorises new forklift and reach-truck operators. No employee drives a counterbalance forklift or reach truck without that personal authorisation, even if trained elsewhere or instructed on pallet jacks. Authorisation is recorded, and daily pre-use checks and MHE faults remain under the maintenance technician and the supervisor on shift.

6. The dispatcher owns dock scheduling. The dispatcher books transport, assigns every carrier a door and a time slot, and coordinates drivers in the marked waiting area. Doors 1-4 are used inbound only and doors 5-8 outbound only. No truck loads or unloads without a dispatcher assignment, and the dispatcher alone releases an outbound load in Zone D for loading and sealing.

7. The shift supervisor on shift owns the floor and immediate incident response. All staff on duty report to that supervisor for task allocation, zone discipline, PPE and speed rules. Any injury, near miss, spill, temperature alarm, equipment fault, rack impact or damage to goods is reported to the supervisor at once, who secures the area, stops unsafe work and ensures the event is recorded.

8. The shift supervisor reviews every incident report from the supervisor's shift. Reports are checked for completeness, follow-up actions and handover to the next shift under PR-15. Where repair, quarantine, recount or retraining is needed, the supervisor assigns it to the maintenance technician, stock controllers, returns staff or operators concerned and checks it is carried out.

9. The shift supervisor approves the final disposition of inspected returns. Returns and packing staff inspect every return in Zone F and propose restock, rework or scrap, but goods only return to stock, go to rework or go to scrap after the supervisor's decision. Returns accepted within 14 days of delivery and damaged goods sent to quarantine the same day they are found are both covered by this approval.

10. Day-to-day ownership stays with the specialist roles. Stock controllers own inventory accuracy, cycle counts, second counts and adjustment proposals. Inbound operators own document and quantity checks in Zone A before release to put-away. The maintenance technician owns trucks, racking and dock equipment and logs every repair. Dispatchers own transport booking and load release. Where ownership overlaps, the shift supervisor decides on the shift and the warehouse manager decides finally.

title: Procedure system PR-01 to PR-15
text:
1. All work at Harborwick 3PL Ltd. runs off fifteen written procedures, PR-01 to PR-15. They are the binding work instructions for every zone, shift and role. Every employee works to the procedures for their task, shift supervisors enforce them on the floor, and the warehouse manager owns them for the site.

2. The procedures cover the full goods flow in order. PR-01 Inbound receiving governs carrier arrival at doors 1-4, document checks before unloading, unloading, counting and inspection in Zone A, and booking and release. PR-02 Put-away to storage governs movement of only booked goods to Zone B, Zone E or Zone F. PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces governs supply of Zone C from bulk storage before each picking shift.

3. Order fulfilment is governed by three further procedures. PR-04 Order picking governs scanner-led picking in Zone C, with scan-verification of every picked item. PR-05 Packing and labelling governs packing, labelling and transfer to Zone D. PR-06 Outbound dispatch governs wrapping, staging in front of doors 5-8, dispatcher release, loading and sealing.

4. Control of stock and goods condition is governed by three procedures. PR-07 Returns handling governs acceptance within 14 days of delivery, inspection of every unit in Zone F, and proposal of restock, rework or scrap. PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts governs daily cycle counts on a rotating schedule, the annual wall-to-wall stocktake, and the rule that no adjustment is posted without a second count. PR-09 Damaged-goods handling governs same-day transfer to quarantine and approved write-off.

5. Safety of people and equipment is governed by two procedures. PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation governs who may drive which truck, authorisation by the warehouse manager, and the documented check before first use each day. PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse governs walkways, crossings, yellow barriers, aisle discipline, the 8 km/h indoor limit with 5 km/h at meeting points, and mandatory high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear.

6. Special goods are governed by two procedures. PR-12 Cold-chain handling governs storage in Zone E between +2 °C and +6 °C, alarms, and manual temperature verification each shift. PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response governs storage only in the ventilated 60 m2 cage in Zone F up to 3,000 kg, handling rules, and spill response.

7. Emergencies and continuity are governed by two procedures. PR-14 Emergency evacuation governs alarms, escape routes, quarterly drills, and roll call at the assembly point by the north fence before anyone re-enters. PR-15 End-of-shift handover governs the 14:00 handover between shift supervisors, covering open doors, unfinished work, staged loads, incidents and equipment defects.

8. No procedure replaces responsibility. The warehouse manager remains accountable for operations, safety and final sign-offs, the shift supervisor on shift remains in charge of the floor and incident response, and the specialist roles retain day-to-day ownership of their tasks. Where a procedure requires an approval or sign-off, the ownership rules in ops.ch02.s2 apply.

9. Procedures are instructed before unsupervised work. No employee carries out inbound, put-away, replenishment, picking, packing, dispatch, returns, counts, MHE operation, cold-chain or hazmat work without instruction in the relevant procedure. Forklift and reach-truck operation additionally requires personal authorisation by the warehouse manager. Floaters work only to procedures they are instructed for.

10. Procedures are fixed and controlled. Only the warehouse manager approves a new version or an exception. Shift supervisors may give zone-level instructions to keep work safe and moving, but may not change a procedure, a limit or an approval threshold. If a procedure and daily instruction appear to conflict, work stops and the shift supervisor clarifies with the warehouse manager before continuing.

title: Carrier arrival and dock assignment
text:
1. All inbound deliveries arrive only through doors 1-4. Doors 1-4 are inbound only and are served from Zone A receiving. Doors 5-8 are outbound only and must never be used for inbound unloading. No inbound truck approaches a door, reverses to a ramp or unloads without a dispatcher assignment.

2. The dispatcher owns dock scheduling for the whole site. Every carrier is booked in advance with a fixed date, time slot and assigned inbound door. The booking covers the carrier name, trailer or van identification, expected pallet count and client goods. Unbooked or early arrivals are not handled out of turn.

3. Carriers report on arrival to the marked driver waiting area in the fenced yard. Drivers remain in the waiting area with their vehicle secured until called to their door. Drivers never enter the hall, enter Zone A, or approach dock doors, levellers or staging areas on foot unless escorted and wearing full PPE.

4. The dispatcher calls each truck to its assigned door in slot order. If a truck misses its slot, it is rebooked to the next free inbound slot by the dispatcher. Shift supervisors do not reassign doors or change the slot order on the floor; where a door is blocked by delay, breakdown or inspection backlog, the supervisor informs the dispatcher, who re-plans doors 1-4.

5. Yard discipline applies from gate to ramp. The speed limit in the yard is 12 km/h, reduced to 5 km/h at the dock ramps, crossings and wherever people and trucks meet. Pedestrian walkways and crossings are used at all times. Manoeuvring takes place only in the marked manoeuvring area, and engines are switched off while waiting at the waiting area and at the door.

6. Each of the 8 dock doors has its own leveller at 1.2 m dock height and is approached only when released by the dispatcher. The driver positions the trailer at the assigned door, secures the vehicle against movement, opens the curtains or rear doors, and returns to the waiting area or designated safe position. Inbound operators then take charge of the door from the Zone A side.

7. Dock approaches and Zone A inspection space are kept clear at all times. No pallets, wrappers, waste or parked handling equipment may block doors 1-4, their approaches, emergency routes or the pedestrian barriers. Main transport aisles of 4.0 m and pedestrian walkways of 1.2 m with yellow barriers remain passable during the whole unloading window.

8. Inbound work takes place only inside operating hours, Monday to Friday 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00, plus approved Saturday morning overtime. Trucks arriving outside shift hours or without overtime approval arranged by the warehouse manager wait outside the schedule and are not unloaded until the next staffed shift. Dock doors are closed and secured outside operating hours.

9. Document control starts before unloading. The carrier hands over delivery notes and transport documents at arrival, and no goods move past Zone A until paperwork is checked under PR-01 Inbound receiving. If documents are missing, refer to the wrong client or differ from the booking, unloading is held and the dispatcher and shift supervisor are informed before any handling begins.

10. Handover at the door is recorded under PR-01 and PR-15. Open inbound doors, trucks still on the ramp, partly unloaded loads and any delay, damage to packaging or incident in the yard are logged and handed from the outgoing to the incoming shift supervisor at 14:00. The next shift continues only the dispatcher-assigned doors and slots, with the same rule: no assignment, no unloading.

title: Documents, unloading and inspection
text:
1. No truck is unloaded until its paperwork is checked and released. The delivery note and transport documents are compared with the dispatcher's booking — carrier, client, pallet and carton quantities, product identities — before any pallet leaves the trailer. If documents are missing, incomplete or do not match the booking, unloading is held.

2. Document checks are done in Zone A by inbound operators under the shift supervisor on shift. The dispatcher provides the expected booking data for doors 1-4. The shift supervisor confirms that door, truck and documents belong together. Only after that confirmation do inbound operators take charge of the load.

3. Any document discrepancy stops the receipt. Wrong client, wrong door or slot, quantity differences on paper, or missing delivery notes are reported at once to the shift supervisor and dispatcher. The truck remains at the door with the load untouched until they decide to rebook, refuse or conditionally receive. No goods move past Zone A while the check is open.

4. Unloading is carried out by instructed operators with suitable equipment only. Counterbalance forklifts, electric pallet jacks and hand pallet jacks are used according to authorisation and capacity, with the 900 kg pallet limit observed. Speed limits of 8 km/h in the hall and 5 km/h at ramps and pedestrian crossings apply throughout. Pallets are placed only in the marked Zone A inspection space.

5. Every delivery is counted as it is unloaded. Inbound operators count pallets and, where the delivery note requires it, outer cartons per pallet, and compare the count with the documents and booking. Counts are recorded under PR-01 Inbound receiving on the WMS scanners. Shortages and overages are noted immediately and not corrected by moving stock from another delivery.

6. Every delivery is inspected as it is counted. Packaging integrity, labelling, pallet condition, cleanliness, signs of leakage, crushing or moisture, and, for date-sensitive food and drugstore goods, dates and batch marks are checked. Chilled goods for Zone E are prioritised and checked against PR-12 Cold-chain handling so the +2 °C to +6 °C chain is not broken.

7. Goods are segregated by inspection result inside Zone A. Goods that pass count and inspection are staged for system booking. Suspect, damaged or unidentifiable goods are separated, marked and kept under control. Damaged goods go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling. Hazmat items are handled only under PR-13 and never stored outside the ventilated cage.

8. Inspection findings are recorded before goods leave Zone A. Pass, hold and quarantine quantities, packaging damage, temperature readings for cold goods, and any incident in unloading are logged under PR-01. The shift supervisor reviews damage and discrepancies on the shift and ensures incident reports, recount requests and quarantine transfers are raised.

9. Only inspected goods are booked into the system, and only booked goods are released to put-away. Inbound operators prepare the passed quantity for booking, stock is booked by scanner to the correct client, and release to Zone B, Zone E or Zone F follows PR-02 Put-away to storage. Uninspected, uncounted or unbooked goods never move to bulk storage, pick faces or dispatch.

10. Partly unloaded trucks, held loads and quarantine transfers are handed over visibly. Open doors 1-4, pallets still on the trailer or in Zone A, and any unresolved document or quality hold are logged and communicated at the 14:00 handover under PR-15. The next shift resumes the same checks from the same point: documents first, then unload, count and inspect.

title: Booking and release to put-away
text:
1. Only goods that have passed document check, count and inspection in Zone A are booked into the system. Uncounted, uninspected or held goods are never booked. Booking is done by WMS scanner against the correct client and delivery, and the system stock is created only at this point.

2. Booking is prepared by inbound operators and completed without delay after inspection. Passed pallets and cartons are staged separately in the marked Zone A booking area, with quantity, product identity, batch and date marks confirmed on the scanner. Suspect, damaged or surplus goods remain segregated and are excluded from the booking quantity.

3. The booking record must match the physical goods staged for put-away. Client, article, quantity, pallet count and, where required, batch, best-before date and temperature reading are entered as verified in Zone A. Shortages and overages against delivery note and dispatcher booking are logged under PR-01 Inbound receiving and are not corrected by adding stock from another delivery.

4. Chilled goods for Zone E are booked with priority. Temperature condition on arrival is recorded under PR-12 Cold-chain handling, and goods outside acceptable condition are not booked to Zone E but held and reported to the shift supervisor. Only goods confirmed as fit for the +2 °C to +6 °C chain are released to the cold zone.

5. Goods requiring special control are booked to Zone F only. Damaged goods go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling and are never booked as available stock. Hazmat items are booked only for the ventilated 60 m2 cage under PR-13, within the 3,000 kg site limit, and never for general storage.

6. Release to put-away follows booking and uses PR-02 Put-away to storage. Only booked goods leave Zone A. Inbound operators label and direct each booked pallet to its destination — Zone B bulk storage, Zone E cold zone, or Zone F services and control — and forklift operators move it by scanner task. Nothing moves to bulk, pick faces or dispatch without this release.

7. Put-away respects the load limits of the destination. Each pallet with load may weigh at most 900 kg. Racking, block-stacking, cold-zone and hazmat-cage limits apply from the moment of release, and overweight, unstable or damaged pallets are not released until repacked or secured.

8. Every booking and release is traceable. Scanner user, time, door 1-4, delivery note reference, booked quantity and put-away destination are recorded in the WMS. The 20 handheld scanners are shared across teams, and each booking is confirmed under the operator's own login so errors can be followed up with stock controllers.

9. Errors found after booking are not corrected by rebooking in Zone A. Any difference between system and physical stock is reported to the shift supervisor and stock controllers for recount under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts. No adjustment is posted without a second count, and write-off approvals under ops.ch02.s2 remain unchanged.

10. Unfinished bookings and releases are handed over visibly at 14:00 under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Booked pallets still in Zone A, held loads awaiting documents or inspection decision, and quarantine transfers not yet moved to Zone F are logged with door, client and quantity. The incoming shift continues from the same point: inspect first, then book, then release.

title: Bulk storage in Zone B
text:
1. Zone B is the bulk reserve store for all ambient goods and covers 2,200 m2. It holds high-bay pallet racking with 2,400 pallet positions, plus marked block-stacking areas for overflow and bulky stock. Only goods booked in Zone A are stored here, and only after release under PR-02 Put-away to storage.

2. Each rack bay carries at most 2,700 kg in total, including pallets and load. This limit is fixed for the rack construction and applies to every bay in Zone B without exception. No bay is ever loaded above 2,700 kg, even if pallet positions in the bay are still free.

3. Every pallet with load may weigh at most 900 kg. That limit governs all put-away to Zone B, because all site capacities are built on it. A bay loaded with full-weight pallets therefore holds at most three pallets at 900 kg each, totalling 2,700 kg and exactly reaching its 2,700 kg limit.

4. Free block-stacking is permitted only in the marked block areas outside the racking. Stacks are limited to 3 pallets high and to 3.5 m total stacking height. No block stack is placed in a transport aisle, a rack aisle, in front of a rack bay, an emergency route or a hydrant, and no stack is leaned against racking.

5. Block-stacked pallets must be stable, uniformly stacked and within the marked floor field. Overweight, leaning, damaged or wrapped-broken pallets are not block-stacked until repacked or rewrapped. Height is measured from the floor to the top of the load, and the 3.5 m limit includes the bottom pallet.

6. Rack storage aisles in Zone B are 3.0 m wide. They serve the high bays and are used by reach trucks rated at 1.6 t and by order of put-away tasks. Main transport aisles crossing or bordering Zone B are 4.0 m wide and are used for through traffic with counterbalance forklifts and pallet jacks. Both widths are kept clear at all times.

7. Aisle discipline is binding in Zone B. Trucks keep to the centre of the aisle, pedestrians use only the marked 1.2 m walkways with yellow barriers and the marked crossings, and no pallet, wrapper foil, scanner equipment or waste is staged in an aisle. Put-away and replenishment stops if an aisle is blocked.

8. Speed limits apply throughout Zone B and are enforced by the shift supervisor. The limit is 8 km/h inside the building, reduced to 5 km/h wherever people and trucks meet, including pedestrian crossings, aisle entries and junctions with the main transport aisles. Pedestrians always have priority.

9. Storage positions are assigned only by WMS scanner task. Forklift and reach-truck operators place each booked pallet only to the position shown on the task and confirm it by scan. No pallet is placed to a free-looking bay, stacked on top of other stock, or moved between bays without a task, so system stock always matches the rack.

10. Racking condition is part of stock safety. Any impact, bent beam, missing pin, leaning pallet or leaking goods in Zone B is reported at once to the shift supervisor and the maintenance technician, the bay is blocked until checked, and the event is recorded. Racking receives a documented safety inspection every month, and damaged bays stay out of use until repaired and released.

title: Put-away process
text:
1. Only goods booked in Zone A leave Zone A for put-away. Uncounted, uninspected, unbooked or held goods never move to storage. Put-away follows PR-02 Put-away to storage and starts only after the WMS booking is complete for the correct client, article and quantity.

2. Every put-away move runs as a WMS scanner task. Inbound operators label and direct each booked pallet to Zone B, Zone E or Zone F, and forklift and reach-truck operators move it only to the position shown on the task and confirm placement by scan. No pallet is placed to a free-looking bay or moved between zones without a task.

3. Destination is fixed by goods type. Ambient reserve stock goes to Zone B bulk storage, chilled goods go to Zone E cold zone, and goods for value-added packing, quarantine, returns handling or hazmat control go to Zone F. Pick faces in Zone C are never a put-away destination; they are supplied only by replenishment under PR-03.

4. Put-away is carried out by authorised operators with suitable equipment only. Counterbalance forklifts rated at 3.0 t handle general moves, reach trucks rated at 2.0 t handle the high bays in Zone B, and electric and hand pallet jacks handle small moves. No one drives a forklift or reach truck without authorisation by the warehouse manager.

5. Every truck used for put-away must have its documented check before first use each day. Trucks with defects, including defective seat belts, faulty brakes, lights or hydraulics, are taken out of use, marked and reported to the shift supervisor and maintenance technician. Forklift operators wear seat belts whenever the truck is moving.

6. Load limits apply at release and at placement. Each pallet with load may weigh at most 900 kg, each rack bay in Zone B carries at most 2,700 kg, and block-stacking outside the racking is limited to 3 pallets high and 3.5 m. Overweight, unstable, leaning or damaged pallets are not put away until repacked or secured.

7. Chilled put-away has priority and runs under PR-12 Cold-chain handling. Goods for Zone E are moved without delay so the +2 °C to +6 °C chain is not broken, placed only to released cold-zone positions, and confirmed by scan with temperature condition recorded. Goods not fit for the cold chain are not put to Zone E but held and reported.

8. Controlled put-away to Zone F runs under PR-09 and PR-13. Damaged goods go to quarantine the same day they are found and are never booked as available stock. Hazmat goes only to the separate ventilated 60 m2 cage, within the 3,000 kg site limit, and never to Zone B, Zone C, Zone D or Zone E.

9. Aisle and speed discipline applies on every put-away run. Main transport aisles are 4.0 m wide, rack storage aisles are 3.0 m wide, and pedestrian walkways are 1.2 m wide with yellow barriers. The limit is 8 km/h inside the building and 5 km/h at crossings, aisle entries and wherever people and trucks meet. Blocked aisles stop put-away until cleared.

10. Unfinished put-away is handed over visibly at 14:00 under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Booked pallets still in Zone A, tasks still open, full or blocked destinations, and any rack impact, spill or equipment fault on the shift are logged with client, quantity and location. The incoming shift continues only from open scanner tasks, with the same rule: no booking, no put-away.

title: Cold storage in Zone E
text:
1. Zone E is the chilled store for temperature-sensitive food, drugstore and household goods and covers 300 m2. It is held continuously between +2 °C and +6 °C. No other temperature range applies, and no ambient, quarantine or hazmat stock is stored in Zone E.

2. Only goods booked in Zone A and released for the cold chain enter Zone E. Put-away follows PR-02 Put-away to storage under PR-12 Cold-chain handling. Uncounted, uninspected, unbooked or temperature-suspect goods are never put to Zone E but are held in Zone A and reported to the shift supervisor.

3. Chilled put-away has priority over ambient put-away. Goods for Zone E are moved without delay after booking so the cold chain is not broken by waiting in Zone A or on a transport aisle. Forklift operators carry them by direct scanner task to the released cold-zone position and confirm placement by scan.

4. Temperature condition on arrival is recorded before booking. Inbound operators check packaging, dates and temperature status under PR-12, and chilled goods outside acceptable condition are not booked to Zone E. They remain segregated, are reported to the shift supervisor, and go to quarantine in Zone F the same day where required.

5. The +2 °C to +6 °C range is monitored by fixed alarms. Any high, low or door-open alarm is reported at once to the shift supervisor on shift, who secures the goods, keeps the cold doors closed and calls the maintenance technician. Affected pallets are not picked, replenished or dispatched until checked and released.

6. A manual temperature verification is carried out every shift in Zone E. The shift supervisor ensures the check is done on both shifts, 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00, and on any approved Saturday overtime when cold stock is held. Readings, time, measuring point and operator login are logged under PR-12 and handed over under PR-15.

7. Cold doors and curtains are kept closed except for immediate put-away, replenishment or picking moves. Doors are not propped open, pallets are not staged in the doorway, and no pallet jack or forklift is parked in the temperature lock. Dwell time in Zone E is limited to the task, and staff wear the provided cold-protection clothing over mandatory high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear.

8. Storage in Zone E follows scanner tasks only. Each booked pallet is placed only to the position shown on the task and confirmed by scan, with client, article, batch and date marks observed for rotation. Every pallet with load may weigh at most 900 kg. Overweight, leaning, damaged or leaking pallets are not stored in Zone E until repacked, and leaks are cleared and reported immediately.

9. Feed of Zone C pick faces for chilled articles comes only from Zone E under PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces. Replenishment runs in small, prompt moves to avoid warming stock in Zone C or in transit. Pickers do not enter Zone E to pick directly, and ambient equipment or packaging is not stored in the cold zone.

10. Unfinished cold work and all temperature events are handed over visibly at 14:00 under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Pallets still to be put away, open alarms, manual readings, blocked positions, and any transfer to quarantine are logged with client, quantity and location. The incoming shift continues only from open scanner tasks, with the same rule: no booking, no cold storage, and no goods outside +2 °C to +6 °C held as available.

title: Hazmat cage and quarantine in Zone F
text:
1. Zone F is the services and control area and covers 600 m2. It holds value-added packing, quarantine for damaged or suspect goods, and returns inspection. Inside Zone F is a separate ventilated hazmat cage of 60 m2. No other zone is used for these control functions.

2. Only goods booked in Zone A and released under PR-02 Put-away to storage enter Zone F for control purposes, except for damaged goods found on site and returns arriving under PR-07. Uncounted or unbooked ambient stock is never put to Zone F, and pick faces in Zone C are never supplied from Zone F.

3. The hazmat cage is the only permitted storage place for hazmat on site. Hazmat never sits in Zone A, Zone B, Zone C, Zone D or Zone E, not even briefly staged or held for a scanner task. Any hazmat item found outside the cage is reported at once to the shift supervisor and moved to the cage under PR-13.

4. The hazmat cage holds at most 3,000 kg in total at any time, including pallets and load. Every pallet with load may weigh at most 900 kg. Cage quantity is checked before every put-away, and no pallet is released to the cage if it would exceed the limit.

5. Put-away to the cage runs only by WMS scanner task under PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response. Forklift operators place each booked pallet only to the position shown on the task and confirm by scan. Incompatible goods are not stored together, the cage is kept locked and ventilated, and access is limited to instructed staff.

6. Quarantine in Zone F holds damaged, suspect, temperature-failed or otherwise blocked goods that are not available stock. Damaged goods go to quarantine the same day they are found under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling, marked, segregated and logged. Quarantined goods are never picked, packed, replenished or dispatched.

7. Returns inspection takes place only in Zone F under PR-07 Returns handling. Returns are accepted within 14 days of delivery, every unit is inspected by returns and packing staff, and restock, rework or scrap is proposed to the shift supervisor. No return re-enters stock without the supervisor's approval of final disposition.

8. Write-off and disposition rules apply from the moment of quarantine. The shift supervisor approves write-offs up to and including 750 EUR and the final disposition of inspected returns. Any write-off above 750 EUR is reserved to the warehouse manager. No adjustment is posted without a second count under PR-08.

9. Spill response, PPE and equipment discipline apply throughout Zone F. Spills are reported at once to the shift supervisor, contained under PR-13, and cleared only with the provided spill means. High-visibility vests and class S3 footwear remain mandatory, trucks keep to 8 km/h inside and 5 km/h at crossings and pedestrian zones, and defective trucks are taken out of use.

10. Unfinished control work is handed over visibly at 14:00 under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Pallets still to be put to quarantine or the cage, cage quantity on hand, open spills, returns awaiting decision, and any transfer to scrap or rework are logged with client, quantity and location. The incoming shift continues only from open scanner tasks and supervisor decisions.

title: Picking zone layout
text:
1. Zone C is the order-picking zone and covers 1,200 m2. It holds ground-level pick faces and flow racks only. No high-bay racking, no block-stacking, no reserve stock and no dispatch staging take place in Zone C. Picking takes place only here.

2. Ground-level pick faces hold the open sales units for ambient goods. Each article has a fixed pick face with marked article, client and location identity. Only one article is held per pick face, and cartons or units are presented forward-facing so pickers can take them without climbing, reaching into racking or moving reserve pallets.

3. Flow racks hold small, fast-moving food, drugstore and household items. Stock is loaded from the rear replenishment side and rolls forward to the pick side by gravity. The pick side faces the picker aisle, the replenishment side faces the feed aisle, and the two sides are never interchanged.

4. All pick faces and flow racks are fed from reserve storage. Ambient faces are replenished only from Zone B bulk storage under PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces. Chilled faces, where provided for Zone E articles, are replenished only from Zone E in small prompt moves under PR-12. Direct put-away from Zone A to Zone C never takes place.

5. Replenishment is completed before each picking shift so every picking shift starts with full faces. Pickers do not pick from empty, half-collapsed or unreplenished faces, and do not fetch reserve stock themselves. If a face runs empty during picking, the picker reports it by scanner and waits for replenishment.

6. Zone C is laid out for picker movement on foot with pallet-jack support. The picker aisles serve the pick sides, the feed aisles serve the rear of the flow racks and the pick-face backs. Main transport aisles bordering or crossing Zone C are 4.0 m wide, internal rack and flow-rack aisles are 3.0 m wide, and marked 1.2 m pedestrian walkways with yellow barriers lead through and out of the zone.

7. Only scanner-assigned stock sits in a pick face or flow lane. Every replenishment is placed by WMS scanner task and confirmed by scan, and every pick is directed by scanner task under PR-04 Order picking. No pallet, carton or return is placed into a pick face without a task, and no stock is moved between faces without a task.

8. Load discipline applies to faces and racks. Every pallet with load may weigh at most 900 kg, and reserve pallets are never stood in the picker aisle or leaned against flow racks. Overweight, leaning, damaged or leaking replenishment is not loaded into Zone C until repacked, and any spill or damage is reported at once to the shift supervisor.

9. Speed, PPE and aisle discipline apply throughout Zone C. Trucks keep to 8 km/h inside the building and 5 km/h wherever people and trucks meet, including aisle entries, crossings and flow-rack feed points. High-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear are mandatory, pedestrians always have priority, and aisles, crossings and escape routes are kept clear at all times.

10. Zone C hands over visibly at 14:00 under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Faces still to be replenished, empty lanes, blocked positions, spills, rack damage and any unfinished picker tasks are logged with client, article and location. The incoming shift starts only from full, scanner-released faces, with the same rule: no replenishment, no picking.

title: Replenishment of pick faces
text:
1. Pick faces and flow racks in Zone C are replenished only from reserve storage under PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces. Ambient faces are fed only from Zone B bulk storage. Chilled faces are fed only from Zone E cold zone. Direct feed from Zone A, Zone D or Zone F to Zone C never takes place.

2. Replenishment is completed before each picking shift. Both shifts, 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00, start picking only from full, scanner-released faces. Replenishment for the morning shift is finished before 06:00, and replenishment for the afternoon shift is finished before 14:00, including any approved Saturday morning overtime.

3. Every replenishment move runs as a WMS scanner task. Stock controllers or the shift supervisor release the tasks by article, quantity and face location. Forklift and reach-truck operators take reserve pallets only from the position shown and place stock only to the face or lane shown, confirming each move by scan. No face is filled without a task.

4. Only booked, available stock is used for replenishment. Quarantined goods, held returns, uninspected goods and blocked pallets are never moved to Zone C. Batch, best-before date and client identity are observed so rotation is maintained, and replenishment follows first-in-first-out unless the scanner task directs otherwise.

5. Replenishment is carried out by authorised operators with suitable equipment only. Counterbalance forklifts rated at 3.0 t handle general feed moves, reach trucks rated at 2.0 t handle retrieval from the high bays in Zone B, and electric and hand pallet jacks handle small forward-fill moves in Zone C. No one drives a forklift or reach truck without authorisation by the warehouse manager.

6. Every truck used for replenishment must have its documented check before first use each day. Trucks with defects are taken out of use, marked and reported to the shift supervisor and maintenance technician. Forklift operators wear seat belts whenever the truck is moving. Each pallet with load may weigh at most 900 kg.

7. Faces and flow lanes are filled to their marked capacity and no further. Reserve pallets are never stood in picker aisles, leaned against flow racks or stacked above faces. Overweight, leaning, damaged or leaking stock is not loaded into Zone C until repacked, and rear-loading sides of flow racks are served only from the feed aisle.

8. Chilled replenishment runs in small, prompt moves under PR-12 Cold-chain handling. Stock is taken from Zone E to the chilled face without waiting in Zone A or on a transport aisle, and cold doors are not propped open. Affected pallets outside +2 °C to +6 °C condition are not replenished but reported to the shift supervisor.

9. Aisle, speed and PPE discipline applies on every replenishment run. Main transport aisles are 4.0 m wide, internal Zone C and rack aisles are 3.0 m wide, and pedestrian walkways are 1.2 m wide with yellow barriers. The limit is 8 km/h inside and 5 km/h at aisle entries, crossings and flow-rack feed points. High-visibility vests and class S3 footwear are mandatory.

10. Unfinished replenishment is handed over visibly at 14:00 under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Faces still to be filled, empty or blocked lanes, reserve positions found empty or damaged, and any spill, rack impact or equipment fault are logged with client, article and location. The incoming shift does not start picking from those faces until replenishment is completed and released.

title: Order picking with scanners
text:
1. Order picking takes place only in Zone C and only against WMS scanner tasks under PR-04 Order picking. Pickers work from ground-level pick faces and flow racks on the pick side only. No picking takes place in Zone B, Zone E or Zone F, and no order is picked from paper, memory or a free-looking face.

2. Pickers start work only from full, scanner-released faces. Replenishment under PR-03 is completed before each picking shift, 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00, so every shift begins with available stock. Pickers never fetch reserve pallets themselves and never fill a face without a replenishment task.

3. Every pick is directed and confirmed by scan. The picker logs in on a handheld WMS scanner under a personal login, follows the task sequence by client, article, quantity and face location, and scans the face location and each picked item or carton. The 20 scanners are shared across teams but tasks remain personal and traceable.

4. Every picked item is scan-verified before it leaves the face. Quantity, article and client identity must match the task on the scanner before the picker confirms. If the scan does not match, the picker stops, leaves the stock in the face and reports to the shift supervisor. Forced confirms, skipped scans and manual corrections without a task are forbidden.

5. Only booked, available stock is picked. Quarantined goods, held returns, blocked pallets, temperature-failed goods and unreplenished faces are never picked. Batch, best-before date and rotation shown on the task are observed, and first-in-first-out applies unless the scanner directs otherwise.

6. If a face runs empty, collapses or shows damage during picking, the picker does not improvise. The empty or faulty lane is reported by scanner, the task is left open, and the picker moves to the next task. Replenishment from Zone B or, for chilled articles, in small prompt moves from Zone E under PR-12, is released by stock controllers or the shift supervisor.

7. Picked goods are handled cleanly to packing. Units and cartons are placed on the picker trolley or pallet without crushing, dragging or mixing clients, kept with labels and dates visible, and passed forward to packing and labelling under PR-05. Overweight, leaning, damaged or leaking stock found in a face is not picked but reported at once.

8. Pickers work on foot with pallet-jack support only as instructed. Electric and hand pallet jacks are used for small moves within capacity, and no picker drives a forklift or reach truck without authorisation by the warehouse manager. High-visibility vests and class S3 footwear are mandatory, pedestrians have priority, and trucks in Zone C keep to 8 km/h and 5 km/h at aisle entries, crossings and flow-rack feed points.

9. Picker aisles, feed aisles, crossings and escape routes are kept clear at all times. Reserve pallets are never stood in picker aisles or leaned against flow racks, and packaging waste, foil and strapping are cleared immediately. Any spill, rack impact, scanner fault or injury is reported at once to the shift supervisor, who secures the area and records the event.

10. Unfinished picking hands over visibly at 14:00 under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Open scanner tasks, empty or blocked faces, replenishment requests, and any damage, spill or equipment defect are logged with client, article and location. The incoming shift continues only from open scanner tasks and full, released faces, with the same rule: no scanner task, no pick, and no pick without scan-verification.

title: Packing and labelling
text:
1. All picked goods pass through packing and labelling under PR-05 Packing and labelling before transfer to Zone D. Picked units and cartons arrive from Zone C by scanner task, are verified, packed, labelled and then wrapped. No picked goods move directly from the pick face to dispatch staging.

2. Packing starts with verification against the scanner task. Packing staff confirm client, order, article, quantity, batch and date marks from the pick, and check that every picked item was scan-verified in Zone C. Mismatched, mixed-client, damaged or short picks are stopped, segregated and reported to the shift supervisor, never packed to complete an order.

3. Packing is carried out at the marked packing stations and, for value-added work, in Zone F. Value-added packing — kitting, display builds, relabelling and client-specific sets — takes place only in Zone F by instructed returns and packing staff. Standard order packing takes place at the packing stations between Zone C and Zone D so packed pallets move forward without backtracking.

4. Only sound pallets, cartons and packing materials are used. Pallets are checked for broken boards, nails and stability, cartons are closed and taped, and loads are stacked uniformly within the pallet footprint without overhang. Every pallet with load may weigh at most 900 kg, and overweight, leaning or unstable pallets are repacked before wrapping.

5. Each packed pallet and carton is labelled before it leaves packing. Labels show client, article, quantity, destination and, where required, batch, best-before date and handling marks exactly as directed by the WMS task. Labels are fixed flat, readable and scan-verifiable, with one label set per pallet. Unlabelled or mislabelled pallets never move to Zone D.

6. Label accuracy is confirmed by scan. Packing staff scan the packed label against the order task on a handheld WMS scanner under personal login, using the shared pool of 20 scanners. A failed scan stops the pallet for recount and relabelling. Forced confirms and handwritten corrections without a task are forbidden.

7. Wrapped pallets only are accepted in Zone D. After labelling, every outbound pallet is wrapped on one of the 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers in dispatch. Wrapping is full, tight and to the pallet foot, with corners and top layer secured. Loose, torn or half-wrapped pallets are rewrapped and are not staged.

8. Cardboard and packaging waste is handled continuously at packing. Empty cartons, dividers and paper are flattened and fed to the single cardboard baler, foil and strapping are collected separately, and waste never accumulates at packing stations, wrappers, aisles or dock approaches. The baler is operated only by instructed staff, and faults are reported at once.

9. Equipment, PPE and aisle discipline apply throughout packing. Wrappers and the baler are used only as instructed, with guards and emergency stops kept in place. High-visibility vests and class S3 footwear are mandatory, trucks and pallet jacks keep to 8 km/h inside and 5 km/h at crossings and pedestrian zones, and packing, wrapper and baler areas are kept clear at all times.

10. Unfinished packing hands over visibly at 14:00 under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Packed, labelled and wrapped pallets awaiting transfer, open packing tasks, label or wrapper faults, and any damage, shortage or incident are logged with client, order and location. The incoming shift continues only from open scanner tasks, with the same rule: no verification, no packing, and no unwrapped or unlabelled pallet to Zone D.

title: Dispatch staging in Zone D
text:
1. Zone D is the outbound staging area and covers 900 m2 in front of docks 5-8. It holds only staged outbound loads awaiting loading. No receiving, bulk storage, picking, quarantine or value-added packing takes place in Zone D, and no inbound truck is ever handled here.

2. Only wrapped and labelled pallets enter Zone D. Every pallet arrives from packing under PR-05 Packing and labelling, fully stretch-wrapped on the semi-automatic wrappers, labelled for client, order, quantity and destination, and scan-confirmed. Unwrapped, unlabelled, mislabelled or unstable pallets are stopped at packing and never staged.

3. Every staged pallet is assigned to a fixed outbound door and load. Dispatchers assign each carrier doors 5-8 with a date and time slot and release the build by WMS scanner task. Pallets are placed only to the marked floor field for their door 5, 6, 7 or 8. No pallet is staged without a door assignment.

4. Staging follows PR-06 Outbound dispatch by scanner task. Packing and forklift staff move each wrapped pallet only to the position shown on the task and confirm placement by scan. Client orders are kept separate by door field, loads are built uniformly without overhang, and every pallet with load may weigh at most 900 kg.

5. Doors 5-8 are outbound only and are controlled by the dispatcher. The dispatcher calls each truck from the marked driver waiting area in slot order, releases the staged load for that door, and authorises loading and sealing. No truck approaches a ramp, docks at a leveller or is loaded without that release.

6. Drivers never enter Zone D or the hall. The driver positions the trailer at the assigned outbound door at 1.2 m dock height, secures the vehicle, opens curtains or rear doors, and returns to the waiting area or designated safe position. Loading is then carried out from the Zone D side by authorised operators.

7. Dock approaches, levellers and transport aisles are kept clear at all times. No wrappers, baler waste, spare pallets or parked jacks may block doors 5-8, their approaches or emergency routes. Main transport aisles of 4.0 m and pedestrian walkways of 1.2 m with yellow barriers remain passable during the whole staging window.

8. Chilled and controlled loads are staged without delay. Goods from Zone E are moved in small prompt moves under PR-12 Cold-chain handling so the +2 °C to +6 °C chain is not broken, and hazmat loads within the 3,000 kg cage limit move only under PR-13. Quarantined, held or unbooked goods are never staged in Zone D.

9. Speed, PPE and equipment discipline apply throughout Zone D. The limit is 8 km/h inside the building, reduced to 5 km/h at dock ramps, crossings and wherever people and trucks meet. High-visibility vests and class S3 footwear are mandatory, pedestrians always have priority, and forklifts, pallet jacks and wrappers are used only as instructed.

10. Unfinished staging hands over visibly at 14:00 under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Staged pallets per door, open build tasks, trucks on the ramp, released and unreleased loads, and any shortage, damage, wrapper fault or incident are logged with door, client, order and quantity. The incoming shift continues only from open scanner tasks and dispatcher-assigned doors, with the same rule: no wrapped and labelled pallet, no staging, and no release, no loading.

title: Load release and truck loading
text:
1. No outbound truck is loaded without dispatcher release under PR-06 Outbound dispatch. Release covers a fixed load for a fixed door 5, 6, 7 or 8, with carrier, date and time slot, client orders, pallet count and destination. Staged pallets in Zone D, even if wrapped and labelled, are not a release.

2. The dispatcher verifies load completeness before release. All pallets for the load are staged in the marked field for the assigned door, scan-confirmed to position, fully stretch-wrapped and labelled for client, order, quantity and destination. Short, mislabelled, unstable or unbooked pallets stop release until corrected at packing.

3. Release respects pallet and vehicle limits. Every pallet with load may weigh at most 900 kg. A contracted curtain-side trailer carries 26,000 kg on 33 floor positions, so at most 28 full-weight pallets per trailer. The delivery van carries 1,800 kg on 6 positions, so only two full-weight pallets go by van and anything heavier goes by trailer.

4. The dispatcher calls the truck from the marked driver waiting area in slot order. The driver positions the trailer at the assigned outbound door at 1.2 m dock height, secures the vehicle against movement, opens the curtains or rear doors, and returns to the waiting area or designated safe position. Drivers never enter Zone D or the hall.

5. Loading is carried out from the Zone D side by authorised operators only. Counterbalance forklifts rated at 3.0 t, electric pallet jacks and hand pallet jacks are used according to authorisation and capacity, with documented daily checks completed. Forklift operators wear seat belts whenever the truck is moving.

6. Every loading move runs as a WMS scanner task under personal login. Operators load in the dispatcher-directed sequence, confirm each pallet by scan from Zone D to trailer, and keep client orders separate without overhang, gaps or mixing. Forced confirms and loading without a task are forbidden. Quarantined, held or unbooked goods are never loaded.

7. Chilled and hazmat loads are loaded without delay under special control. Goods from Zone E move in small prompt steps under PR-12 Cold-chain handling so the +2 °C to +6 °C chain is not broken. Hazmat moves only under PR-13 within the 3,000 kg cage limit, never with incompatible goods, and never outside the released quantity.

8. The loaded trailer is checked before sealing. Pallet count, stability, wrapping integrity, label match to the release and even weight distribution are verified on the leveller, and the dispatcher confirms the count against the WMS. Shortages, overages or damage found at the ramp stop sealing and are reported to the shift supervisor.

9. Sealing and documents close the load. After dispatcher approval the trailer curtains or doors are closed, the load is sealed, and transport documents and delivery notes are handed to the driver at the door. Seal number, time, door, carrier and pallet count are logged in the WMS. An unsealed or undocumented trailer never leaves the ramp.

10. Open doors, trucks on the ramp and sealed departures hand over visibly at 14:00 under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Released and unreleased loads per door 5-8, pallets still to load, trucks waiting in the yard, seal numbers issued, and any delay, damage, wrapper fault or incident are logged with door, client, order and quantity. Work continues only on dispatcher-assigned doors, and doors are closed and secured outside operating hours.

title: Pallet weight and trailer capacity
text:
1. Every pallet with load may weigh at most 900 kg. That weight includes the wooden pallet, cartons, units, wrapping foil and label. It is the governing unit load for the whole site, and every storage, handling and transport capacity is calculated from it.

2. The 900 kg limit applies at packing, at staging and at loading. Packing staff build every outbound pallet within the pallet footprint without overhang, check stability and wrapping, and stop any overweight, leaning or unstable pallet before it leaves packing under PR-05 Packing and labelling.

3. No overweight pallet enters Zone D or a trailer. A pallet found above 900 kg in packing, in staging or at the ramp is returned for repacking into two pallets. The dispatcher never releases a load containing an overweight pallet, and operators never load one to work around the limit.

4. Our contracted curtain-side trailers carry at most 26,000 kg of payload on 33 floor pallet positions. Both numbers apply together: the trailer is full when either the weight limit or the floor-position limit is reached first. The 33 positions are floor places for standard pallets loaded single-height.

5. For full-weight pallets the weight limit governs, not the floor space. At 900 kg per pallet, 26,000 kg divided by 900 kg gives 28.88, so at most 28 pallets. A trailer loaded with full-weight pallets therefore takes at most 28 pallets, and the remaining 5 floor positions stay empty because the weight limit is already reached.

6. For lighter pallets the floor limit can govern instead. Pallets below 900 kg use less of the 26,000 kg allowance, so more than 28 pallets may be loaded until either limit is met. In no case is more than 33 pallets loaded to one trailer, and in no case is more than 26,000 kg loaded, even if positions remain free.

7. Load planning uses the heavier calculation for every order. The dispatcher checks total load weight as number of pallets multiplied by verified pallet weight against the 26,000 kg limit, and checks pallet count against the 33-position limit. A load passes only when both checks pass under PR-06 Outbound dispatch.

8. Weight is distributed evenly over the trailer bed. Full-weight pallets are spread from front to rear without gaps, overhang or stacking, secured by the trailer curtains, and confirmed by scan from Zone D to trailer. Uneven, concentrated or shifting loads are stopped at the leveller and reloaded before sealing.

9. The trailer limit is independent of storage limits but built on the same pallet. The 2,700 kg rack-bay limit, the 3-high and 3.5 m block-stack limit, the 3.0 t forklift rating and the wrapper discipline all assume the same maximum 900 kg unit. An overweight pallet therefore breaks storage, handling and transport safety at once.

10. Unfinished trailer calculations hand over visibly at 14:00 under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Planned and released pallet counts per door 5-8, verified weights, trailers already sealed and trailers still to load are logged with door, client, order and quantity. The incoming shift loads only dispatcher-released quantities within the 28-pallet, 26,000 kg and 33-position limits.

title: Van and shift dispatch limit
text:
1. The delivery van carries at most 1,800 kg of payload on 6 floor pallet positions. Both numbers apply together: the van is full when either the weight limit or the floor-position limit is reached first. The 6 positions are floor places for standard pallets loaded single-height.

2. For full-weight pallets the weight limit governs, not the floor space. At 900 kg per pallet, two full-weight pallets use 1,800 kg of the 1,800 kg allowance and leave 0 kg free. A third full-weight pallet would need 2,700 kg in total and exceeds the limit, so the van takes only two full-weight pallets.

3. The remaining 4 floor positions on a van carrying two full-weight pallets stay empty for weight reasons. They are not filled with additional full pallets, part-pallets counted as full weight, or extra cartons that would take the load above 1,800 kg. The dispatcher never releases a van load above 1,800 kg.

4. For lighter pallets the floor limit can govern instead. Pallets well below 900 kg use less of the 1,800 kg allowance, so more than two pallets may be loaded until either limit is met. In no case is more than 6 pallets loaded to one van, and in no case is more than 1,800 kg loaded, even if positions remain free.

5. Anything heavier than the van limit goes by trailer. Any single pallet above 900 kg is already an overweight pallet and is repacked before dispatch, and any order above 1,800 kg total, or requiring more than two full-weight pallets, is planned to a contracted curtain-side trailer under ops.ch07.s1. Vans are never overloaded to avoid a trailer movement.

6. Van loads are planned, staged and released like trailer loads. The dispatcher checks total weight as number of pallets multiplied by verified pallet weight against the 1,800 kg limit, and checks pallet count against the 6-position limit under PR-06 Outbound dispatch. Vans are loaded at an assigned door 5-8 by scanner task, confirmed by scan, checked and sealed before departure.

7. The site operates 4 outbound doors, doors 5-8, for shift dispatch. Each outbound door handles at most 4 trailer loads per shift. That rate covers call-forward, positioning at the 1.2 m leveller, scan-confirmed loading from Zone D, check and sealing, and departure within the Monday to Friday shifts 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00, plus any approved Saturday morning overtime.

8. At full-weight pallets this door rate fixes the maximum promise per shift. Four trailer loads per door multiplied by 4 doors gives 16 trailer loads per shift. At 28 full-weight pallets per trailer, 16 multiplied by 28 gives 448 full-weight pallets per shift. That is the most we can promise a client for one shift.

9. The 448-pallet figure is a promise limit, not a staging target. It applies to full-weight pallets at 900 kg each, totalling 403,200 kg across 16 trailers. For lighter pallets more pallets per trailer may be possible within the 26,000 kg and 33-position limits, but the dispatcher never promises above 448 full-weight equivalents per shift, and never plans more than 16 trailer departures per shift.

10. Unfinished van and shift quantities hand over visibly at 14:00 under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Planned and released van loads with verified weights, trailers loaded per door 5-8 against the 4-per-door rate, and progress toward the 448-pallet limit are logged with door, client, order and quantity. The incoming shift continues only within the remaining door capacity and the van limits of 1,800 kg and 6 positions.

title: Hazmat cage pallet limit
text:
1. The ventilated hazmat cage inside Zone F holds at most 3,000 kg in total at any time, including pallets and load. This limit covers all hazmat on site together. It applies continuously, on both shifts 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00 and on any approved Saturday morning overtime.

2. The cage is the only permitted storage place for hazmat on site and measures 60 m2. Hazmat never sits in Zone A, Zone B, Zone C, Zone D or Zone E, not even briefly staged for a scanner task. Any hazmat item found outside the cage is reported at once to the shift supervisor and moved under PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response.

3. Every pallet with load may weigh at most 900 kg. That unit weight includes the wooden pallet, containers, absorbents, wrapping and labels. It is the same governing unit load as in the rest of the site, and the cage capacity is calculated from it.

4. For full-weight pallets the weight limit governs, not the floor space. At 900 kg per pallet, 3,000 kg divided by 900 kg gives 3.33, so at most 3 pallets. The cage therefore takes at most 3 full-weight pallets, and a fourth full-weight pallet is refused because it would take the total to 3,600 kg above the weight limit.

5. No pallet is released to the cage if it would exceed the limit. Cage quantity on hand is checked before every put-away under PR-02 Put-away to storage. A load passes only when current stock plus the new pallet weight is at or below 3,000 kg, confirmed by scanner task. The dispatcher never plans and the supervisor never approves above the limit.

6. For lighter pallets the weight check governs in the same way. Pallets below 900 kg use less of the 3,000 kg allowance, but in no case is more than 3,000 kg held, even if floor positions inside the cage remain free. Incompatible goods are never stored together to use the remaining allowance, and the cage is kept locked and ventilated.

7. Put-away and removal run only by WMS scanner task under PR-13. Forklift operators place each booked pallet only to the position shown and confirm by scan, and removals for dispatch, rework or scrap are confirmed in the same way. No pallet is placed to a free-looking space or moved between the cage and another zone without a task.

8. Overweight, unstable, leaking, damaged or unlabelled pallets never enter the cage. A pallet found above 900 kg is repacked before control, and leaking or damaged hazmat is contained, reported to the shift supervisor and handled under spill response. Access is limited to instructed staff wearing mandatory high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear.

9. Dispatch from the cage respects the same calculation. Hazmat loads are released by the dispatcher under PR-06 Outbound dispatch only within the quantity on hand, moved without delay, never mixed with incompatible goods, and loaded at the assigned door 5-8 by scanner task. Quarantined or unbooked hazmat is never loaded.

10. Cage quantities hand over visibly at 14:00 under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Quantity on hand against the 3,000 kg limit, pallets stored as full-weight equivalents toward the 3-pallet limit, open tasks, pending removals, spills and access events are logged with client, quantity and location. The incoming shift continues only within the remaining weight allowance.

title: Daily cycle counts
text:
1. Cycle counts run every working day, Monday to Friday, on a rotating zone schedule under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts. Counting never stops: each working day a defined part of the site is counted, so Zone A, Zone B, Zone C, Zone D, Zone E and Zone F, including quarantine and the hazmat cage, are covered in rotation without interrupting receiving, put-away, replenishment, picking or dispatch.

2. Stock controllers own daily cycle counts. The two stock controllers plan the rotating schedule, release count tasks by WMS scanner, carry out first and second counts, investigate differences between system and rack, and prepare adjustments for approval. They work closely with inbound, picking, returns and dispatch staff so counted areas remain stable while the count is open.

3. Every count runs as a WMS scanner task under personal login. Counters use the shared pool of 20 handheld scanners, log in individually, follow the task by client, article, quantity and location, and confirm each location by scan. Paper, memory or free-looking checks are not counts, and forced confirms without scanning the physical stock are forbidden.

4. Counted areas are frozen for movement while the count is open. The shift supervisor ensures no put-away, replenishment, picking, packing transfer or dispatch move takes goods into or out of the locations under count until the task is closed. Booked pallets still in Zone A, staged pallets in Zone D and replenishment in progress are excluded from the open count and logged separately.

5. The first count compares physical stock with system stock at the location. Client, article, quantity, pallet count and, where required, batch, best-before date and temperature status are verified. Cold goods in Zone E are counted promptly so the +2 °C to +6 °C chain is not broken, and hazmat in the 60 m2 cage is counted only under PR-13 without moving pallets between positions.

6. No adjustment is ever posted without a second count. Any location where first count and system differ is recounted by a second person, normally the other stock controller or the shift supervisor, on a fresh scanner task. The recount is independent: the second counter does not see the first result before counting.

7. If second count matches system, the first count is treated as a count error and no adjustment follows. If second count matches the first count, a real discrepancy exists and is investigated: open put-away tasks, unfinished replenishment, packing or staging moves, returns awaiting decision in Zone F, and quarantine transfers the same day are checked before any adjustment is proposed.

8. Damaged, quarantined and blocked stock is never counted as available. Goods in quarantine in Zone F, held returns, temperature-failed pallets and unbooked goods in Zone A are counted separately as blocked quantities. They do not adjust available system stock, and write-off rules apply: the shift supervisor approves write-offs up to and including 750 EUR, the warehouse manager approves anything above 750 EUR per case.

9. Every count, recount and proposed adjustment is recorded in the WMS with scanner user, time, zone, location, client, article and quantities. The shift supervisor reviews discrepancies found on the shift, ensures incident reports, recount requests and quarantine transfers are raised, and hands open counts to the next shift. Count tasks are closed daily; no count stays open overnight between 22:00 and 06:00.

10. Unfinished and disputed counts hand over visibly at 14:00 under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Locations counted, locations still to count in the day's rotation, double-counted locations awaiting second count, and adjustments awaiting sign-off are logged with zone, location, client and quantity. The incoming shift continues only from open scanner tasks, with the same rule: no second count, no adjustment.

title: Annual wall-to-wall stocktake
text:
1. Once a year the site shuts down for a full wall-to-wall stocktake under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts. All locations in Zones A to F are counted wall to wall — bulk racking and block stocks in Zone B, pick faces and flow racks in Zone C, staging in Zone D, cold stock in Zone E, quarantine, returns and the ventilated 60 m2 hazmat cage in Zone F — including blocked, quarantined and held quantities counted separately.

2. During the stocktake all goods movement stops. No receiving at doors 1-4, no put-away, no replenishment, no picking, no packing transfer and no loading at doors 5-8 take place until the count is closed.
